I want to add a new class for IsUnital which literally just says that a multiplicative type is unital. Obviously this will come with a note:

/-- A multiplicative magma is **unital** if there exists a unit.

**Note**: Do not use this unless it is the only reasonable way to phrase or prove a statement.
In general you should use `NonUnitalRing`, `Ring`, etc. -/
@[mk_iff] class IsUnital (A : Type*) [Mul A] : Prop where
  isUnital : ∃ u : A, ∀ x : A, u * x = x ∧ x * u = x

So this is just a Prop-version of docs#MulOneClass.

Sometimes it's useful to use such a definition in a statement, for example, in #36327, we show that a C*-algebra is unital iff the set of extreme points in the closed unit ball is nonempty.

I wanted to see if there were any objections to add such a class before I start upstreaming this.

I want the statement to be IsUnital A ↔ _. With MulOneClass, you'd need to have separate statements and definitions for One, MulOneClass, and then use that to build your algebra, which is less than ideal (especially if we want to do this for another statement).
In your existence definition, you may have to prove it is unique later because the later in the definiton of algebra you will have to provide the choice. Is this really what you want?

Monica Omar said:

then use that to build your algebra, which is less than ideal

I don't understand this. To build up an algebra, you would have to provide a unit. In you existence definition, you will have to use `obtain \<u, hu\> := IsUnital A. But it is less clear that your resulting algebra structure does not depend on this choice of unit.

If you change your definition in to existence and uniquensee statement, then it simply suggests that the essense of your proof should be constructional, for which you might not want it to be a Prop.

Let me know if the following is something you want:

Class YourClass : Prop := `the set of extreme points in the closed unit ball is nonempty`

instance [YourClass] : algebra C YourC*Algebra where
  one := sorry
...

You can construct the unit explicitly, and we do, but the construction works using any extreme point, so there isn't really a preferred one.

Regardless if this initial use case, I think we want IsUnital anyway. Note that in the context of Gelfand duality, we already have the corresponding notion (and its negation) for topological spaces: docs#CompactSpace and docs#NoncompactSpace.

There are some things which can only be stated properly using this class. For example, the minimal unitization, as an extension of C\*-algebras, is split exact if and only if the algebra is unital (i.e., IsUnital A).

So, the point is not to build an Algebra (although you would also provide that constructor, to be used only rarely and generally mid-proof), but rather to be able to make statements involving it. Without this class, you can't fill in the right hand side of "a C\*-algebra does not possess an extreme point of the closed unit ball if and only if ..." in a satisfactory manner.

Jireh Loreaux said:

You can construct the unit explicitly, and we do, but the construction works using any extreme point, so there isn't really a preferred one.

Sorry, I am not an expert at all, still confused. If the unit exists, it has to be canonical right there since it would be unique. If you cannot construct your unit canonically, you will still be in the trouble of non-definitionally-equal algebra structures in Lean, right? I am not sure if this matters for you.

Indeed, that's why Jireh Loreaux said:

So, the point is not to build an Algebra (although you would also provide that constructor, to be used only rarely and generally mid-proof)

Jireh Loreaux said:

Indeed, that's why Jireh Loreaux said:

So, the point is not to build an Algebra (although you would also provide that constructor, to be used only rarely and generally mid-proof)

If I understand correctly, probably we agree that we want the class IsUnital alone if the point is to make your desired statement able to be stated. The IsUnital.toMulOneClass in #41923 seems abusing classical.choose to me (which might lead to coherence nightmare if abused and your previous answer didn't address this issue). If you have to make some choice of an extreme point, why not record it as part of data by the constructional nature to get rid of classical.choose in the statement?
For example :

def YourUnitConstructor (x : ExtremePoints) : MulOneClass YourC*Algebra where
  one := sorry
...

I think this will make the use of classical.choose transparent and seperate the noncomputatble part, instead of letting classical.choose be hidden in IsUnital.toMulOneClass.

Your comment is not without merit, but I think it's still missing the intended use case. The merit comes from the fact that @Monica Omar needs to emphasize in the docstrings of IsUnital.toSomeUnitalFoo that these constructors should almost never be used in practice because they create bad definitional equalities (for 1, but also Pow ℕ and other fields only present in unital structures) and are primarily intended for ephemeral use within a proof.

Jiaxi Mo said:

If you have to make some choice of an extreme point, why not record it as part of data by the constructional nature to get rid of classical.choose in the statement?

Because even the extreme point itself is obtained through Nonempty.some in the application we have. In particular, von Neumann algebras are characterized among all (possibly non-unital) C⋆-algebras as those possessing a Banach predual. However, all von Neumann algebras are in fact unital. How does one show this? Well, by showing that the collection of extreme points of the closed unit ball is nonempty using Krein-Milman and the weak⋆ topology relative to the predual.

Jireh Loreaux said:

Because even the extreme point itself is obtained through Nonempty.some in the application we have.

What I wanted to emphasize is that it seems better to record the use of classical.choose where you actually meet Nonempty.someand get another place to record the construction of unit which works for any given point and should be computatble. Why does this not satisfy the intended use case? I am not saying NO to any usage of classical.choose. I just felt like at least do not let the choice happen inIsUnital.toMulOneClass, if the "choice" actually comes from C*algebra arguments.

Sorry again, I am totally ignorant the this mathematical area, so please forgive me if I am talking about something unrelated to the application in reality.

Jiaxi Mo said:

I just felt like at least do not let the choice happen inIsUnital.toMulOneClass, if the "choice" actually comes from C*algebra arguments.

Because there may be different C⋆-algebraic arguments that lead you to the existence (propositionally) of a unit, and then it's nice to have a single constructor. Moreover, this is applicable outside C⋆-algebras too (e.g., you can have a semigroup which you can prove mid-proof has an identity, and then you upgrade it to a monoid) so there is no reason to restrict identity creation to C⋆-algebras. Ultimately IsUnital plays as similar role as docs#IsField, but in different contexts.

docs#IsField does not attach addition data like MulOne. Could you please give me an example outside C⋆-algebras which you can prove mid-proof has an identity, and then you upgrade it to a monoid where you have to use classical.choose to make the unit?

I think docs#IsField.toField (or rather, docs#IsField.toSemifield which actually constructs the inverse data) is pretty analogous here
